papers.note: A review of 146 studies from 2007 to 2018 finds AI in higher education concentrated in computer science and four application areas, with little critical reflection on risks or pedagogical theory, so educators remain largely absent from shaping how these tools affect teaching and learning.
papers.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
papers.authors: Olaf Zawacki‐Richter, Victoria I. Marín, Melissa Bond, Franziska Gouverneur
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looked at many studies about artificial intelligence in universities, published between 2007 and 2018. The authors started with 2656 papers and narrowed them down to 146 for a close look. They found that most of this research comes from computer science and related fields, not from education. The tools studied mostly do four things: predict student success, grade or evaluate work, adapt to each learner, or act as tutoring systems. The paper warns that risks and ethics get little attention, and teachers are rarely involved in shaping these tools.
papers.explain_business: This review of 146 studies from 2007 to 2018 shows that AI in higher education is still driven mainly by computer science and STEM researchers, with little input from educators. The tools cluster around predicting student outcomes, assessment, personalisation, and tutoring. Risks, ethics, and pedagogical theory receive scant attention. For leaders, this signals that adoption decisions should not rely on technical research alone. Investment in AI should include educators in design and governance, and should fund evaluation of ethical and teaching impact, not just deployment of prediction, assessment, or tutoring systems.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic review of AI in higher education, screening 2656 publications from 2007 to 2018 and synthesizing 146 articles using explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. Descriptive analysis showed that computer science and STEM dominate the field, and empirical work relies mostly on quantitative methods. The synthesis identified four application areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The authors conclude that critical reflection on challenges and risks is largely absent, links to pedagogical theory are weak, and ethical and educational approaches need more exploration.

papers.note: The paper argues that combining cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence now makes computer tutors as effective as human tutors, showing working systems for geometry proofs and LISP programming, which matters because it grounds AI in education in tested learning theory.
papers.title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems
papers.authors: John R. Anderson, C. Franklin Boyle, Brian J. Reiser
papers.explain_beginner: This paper says that computers can now teach students as well as human tutors can. The authors built tutoring programs using ideas from psychology about how people learn. One program helped students with geometry proofs, and another helped them write computer programs in LISP. The paper argues that combining thinking research and artificial intelligence makes this possible. This matters because it shows computer tutors can be grounded in tested learning theory, not just guesswork, so students might get effective teaching from machines.
papers.explain_business: This paper indicates that computer-based tutoring can now match human tutors in effectiveness. The authors built working tutors for geometry proofs and LISP programming, using principles from cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence. For decision makers, this means investing in AI tutoring systems grounded in learning theory could deliver quality instruction at scale, potentially reducing reliance on human tutors for certain subjects. It informs choices about where to apply AI in education and supports prioritizing tools built on validated cognitive models rather than ad hoc software.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors argue that cognitive psychology, artificial intelligence, and computer technology have matured enough to build computer tutors matching intelligent human tutors. They developed tutors based on pedagogical principles from the ACT theory of cognition. These systems were built for two domains: teaching students to do geometry proofs and teaching them to write LISP programs. The key result is that such tutors are feasible and effective, demonstrating that grounding instructional design in a cognitive theory can produce working tutoring systems for real tasks.

papers.note: The paper argues universities should respond to ChatGPT with clear policies, staff training and detection methods rather than bans, because the tool offers real benefits alongside cheating risks, which matters as institutions decide how to govern AI in teaching and assessment.
papers.title: Chatting and cheating: Ensuring academic integrity in the era of ChatGPT
papers.authors: Debby Cotton, Peter A. Cotton, J. Reuben Shipway
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at ChatGPT in universities and asks whether it helps or hurts learning. It says the tool can get students more involved, working together, and able to access help more easily. But it also makes cheating and copying easier to do. The authors argue that banning ChatGPT is not the best answer. Instead, universities should make clear rules, train staff, and use ways to spot cheating. The main point is that schools can handle the risks if they act early and focus on honest use.
papers.explain_business: For leaders in education, this paper says ChatGPT brings real benefits and real risks, so a simple ban is not the right move. The authors recommend clear policies, staff training, and detection methods to support honest use. This informs decisions about how to govern AI in teaching and assessment. Instead of blocking the tool, institutions should set rules, build staff capability, and put checks in place. That way they can protect academic integrity while still allowing the engagement, collaboration, and accessibility benefits the paper describes.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper reviews both the upsides and downsides of ChatGPT in higher education. It notes benefits such as student engagement, collaboration, and accessibility, alongside concerns about academic honesty and plagiarism. The authors examine why detecting and preventing dishonest use is hard, then propose strategies for ethical use. These include creating policies and procedures, offering training and support, and applying detection and prevention methods. The conclusion is that a proactive, ethical approach lets universities manage the challenges while still gaining the opportunities the tool provides.

papers.note: This review found that human tutoring helps students far less than commonly believed, and that intelligent tutoring systems are nearly as effective, which matters because it suggests schools can rely on software for tutoring gains at much lower cost.
papers.title: The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems
papers.authors: Kurt A. VanLehn
papers.explain_beginner: This review looked at studies that compared students who received tutoring with students who learned the same material without tutoring. People often assume human tutors are far better than computer programs. The review found this is not true. Human tutoring produced a moderate improvement, and computer tutoring systems designed to respond step by step produced almost the same improvement. This matters because it suggests schools may get similar learning benefits from software as from human tutors, which could make extra help available to more students at lower cost.
papers.explain_business: Leaders often assume that only human tutors deliver strong learning gains and that software is a weak substitute. This review of comparison studies found otherwise. Human tutoring improved outcomes by a moderate amount, and intelligent tutoring systems achieved almost the same result. The practical implication is that software based tutoring can deliver learning benefits close to those of human tutors, likely at much lower cost and with easier scaling. This informs decisions about where to invest limited instructional budgets, suggesting that intelligent tutoring software deserves serious consideration alongside human tutoring programs.
papers.explain_practitioner: The author reviewed experiments comparing human tutoring, computer tutoring, and instruction covering the same content without tutoring. Computer systems were grouped by interaction granularity: answer-based, step-based, and substep-based. Intelligent tutoring systems typically use step or substep interaction, while other systems use answer-based interfaces. The common belief was that finer granularity yields larger effects, with expected effect sizes of 0.3, 1.0, and 2.0 for answer-based systems, intelligent tutoring systems, and adult human tutors. The review did not confirm this. Human tutoring measured 0.79, and intelligent tutoring systems measured 0.76, nearly equal.

papers.note: A survey of 399 Hong Kong university students found generally positive views of generative AI for personalized learning and writing support, but also concerns about accuracy, privacy, ethics and career impact, so educators and policymakers should address these worries when integrating such tools.
papers.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
papers.authors: Cecilia Ka Yuk Chan, Wenjie Hu
papers.explain_beginner: This paper asked 399 university students in Hong Kong how they feel about generative AI tools like ChatGPT. Most students had a positive view. They saw these tools as helpful for learning in ways suited to them, for writing, for sharing ideas, and for research and analysis. At the same time, students worried about whether the tools give correct information, about privacy, about ethics, and about how the tools might affect their personal growth, their future jobs, and society's values. The paper matters because it shows that students are open to these tools but also have real concerns that schools and policymakers should take seriously.
papers.explain_business: This study surveyed 399 Hong Kong university students and found broad openness to generative AI in learning, with students valuing personalized support, writing help, and research assistance. However, students also flagged risks around accuracy, privacy, ethics, and impacts on personal development, careers, and societal values. For executives in education or edtech, the practical message is that adoption can move forward, but trust and safeguards matter as much as features. The decision this informs is how to roll out generative AI: invest in accuracy checks, privacy protections, and clear ethical guidelines, and involve students in shaping policy, rather than treating the technology as a simple add-on.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors surveyed 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students across disciplines in Hong Kong to map their perceptions of generative AI in higher education. The study examined familiarity, willingness to engage, perceived benefits and challenges, and views on effective integration. Students were generally positive, citing personalized learning support, writing and brainstorming help, and research and analysis capabilities. They also raised concerns about accuracy, privacy, ethics, and effects on personal development, career prospects, and societal values. Framing the findings through Biggs' 3P model, the authors argue that student perceptions shape learning approaches and outcomes, so educators and policymakers should use these insights to design responsible integration guidelines.

papers.note: The paper argues that AI is becoming embedded in university teaching, learning, support and administration, and that institutions must address adoption challenges to shape how higher education evolves, which matters to anyone tracking AI's growing role in education.
papers.title: Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education
papers.authors: Ştefan Popenici, Sharon Kerr
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how artificial intelligence is starting to appear in universities, not just in one area but across teaching, learning, student support, and administration. The authors ask what this means for how students learn and how universities operate and change over time. They note that new technology is arriving quickly and being adopted faster than before. The main point is that universities face real challenges in adopting AI well, and that these choices will shape what higher education becomes. This matters because AI is becoming a normal part of university life.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper signals that artificial intelligence is spreading through universities in teaching, learning, student support, and administration, and that adoption is speeding up. The authors argue that institutions must actively address the challenges of adopting these technologies, because those choices will influence how higher education develops. In practice, this means leaders should treat AI adoption as a strategic issue that touches many parts of the institution, not a single department's project. The decision it informs is whether and how to plan for AI adoption deliberately, so the institution helps shape its future rather than reacting to it.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors examine the emergence of artificial intelligence in higher education and its educational implications for student learning and institutional teaching and evolution. They consider recent technological advances and the accelerating adoption of new technologies in universities, then use these trends to anticipate the future character of higher education where AI is embedded throughout the institution. The paper identifies challenges that institutions and student learning face when adopting these technologies across teaching, learning, student support, and administration, and it outlines directions for further research. The key contribution is framing adoption challenges and a research agenda rather than reporting experimental results.

papers.note: This review found ChatGPT's accuracy varies by subject, strong in economics but weak in maths, and can assist teaching while risking fake information and plagiarism, so schools should update assessments, policies and training now.
papers.title: What Is the Impact of ChatGPT on Education? A Rapid Review of the Literature
papers.authors: Chung Kwan Lo
papers.explain_beginner: A review looked at early research on ChatGPT in education, covering December 2022 to February 2023. It found the chatbot's accuracy depends on the subject. It did very well in economics, was okay at programming, and struggled with mathematics. ChatGPT can help teachers create materials and give students a virtual tutor for questions and group work. But it can also produce false information and let students avoid plagiarism checks. The review says schools and universities should act quickly to change how they assess students, update their rules, and train both teachers and students.
papers.explain_business: This review shows ChatGPT's reliability depends on the subject, strong in economics, weaker in maths, which matters for any organization using it in training or education products. It can support instructors and learners, but it can also generate false information and help users evade plagiarism checks. The practical implication is that schools and universities should not wait. Leaders should update assessment methods and institutional policies now, and invest in training for instructors and students. This informs decisions about adopting AI tools, managing academic integrity risk, and funding staff and student readiness programs.
papers.explain_practitioner: This rapid review analyzed 50 articles from relevant databases and Google Scholar, published December 2022 to February 2023, using open, axial, and selective coding. It examined ChatGPT's capabilities across subjects, educational uses, and researcher-identified issues. Performance ranged from outstanding in economics to satisfactory in programming to unsatisfactory in mathematics. The tool can assist instructors with course materials and suggestions, and act as a virtual tutor answering questions and supporting collaboration. Challenges include incorrect or fake information and bypassing plagiarism detectors. The author recommends immediate updates to assessment methods and institutional policies, plus instructor training and student education.

papers.note: This early review argues ChatGPT can produce human-like prose that threatens traditional assessment, so universities should rethink how they evaluate learning, weighing both opportunities and risks for students, teachers and institutions.
papers.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
papers.authors: Jürgen Rudolph, Samson Tan, Shannon Tan
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at ChatGPT, a chatbot that can write surprisingly human-like text in seconds. The authors reviewed existing research and tried the tool themselves. They found that ChatGPT could make traditional ways of testing students, like essays and exams done at home, much harder to trust. The paper says universities need to rethink how they check what students have learned. It also points out both possible benefits and risks for students, teachers and schools. The main message is that assessment must change because AI writing tools are here to stay.
papers.explain_business: For executives in higher education, this paper signals that AI chatbots like ChatGPT can produce convincing written work, which undermines conventional assessment such as take-home essays. The authors recommend that institutions rethink how they evaluate learning and consider both opportunities and risks for students, teachers and the organisation. The decision this informs is whether to invest in new assessment methods, staff training and policies around AI use. It also highlights OpenAI's shift from non-profit to commercial business, showing that AI tools will keep advancing, so institutions should act rather than wait.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted an extensive literature review and hands-on experiments with ChatGPT, a variant of OpenAI's GPT language model. They describe its functionality, strengths and limitations, then position it within Artificial Intelligence in Education research. They examine student-facing, teacher-facing and system-facing applications and analyse opportunities and threats. The paper is among the first peer-reviewed journal articles on ChatGPT in higher education. It concludes with recommendations for students, teachers and institutions, many focused on assessment. The key result is that ChatGPT's human-like prose threatens traditional assessment, so evaluation methods need rethinking.

papers.note: This review of 138 studies from 2016 to 2022 finds AI in higher education growing fast, led by China and education departments, mostly used for assessment, prediction, tutoring and managing learning, which shows where the field is heading and what remains unstudied.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
papers.authors: Helen Crompton, Diane Burke
papers.explain_beginner: This paper reviewed 138 studies about artificial intelligence in higher education from 2016 to 2022. It found that publications grew very quickly in 2021 and 2022, rising two to three times above earlier years. Research happened on six continents, and China replaced the US as the leader. Education departments became the main source of researchers. Most studies focused on undergraduate students and on language learning. AI was mostly used for assessment, prediction, tutoring, helping as an assistant, and managing student learning. The review also points to gaps, including newer tools like ChatGPT, showing where future research could go.
papers.explain_business: This review of 138 studies shows AI in higher education is expanding fast, especially in 2021 and 2022, with China now leading research output. Most work targets undergraduate students and language learning, and the main uses are assessment, prediction, tutoring, AI assistance, and managing learning. For executives, this signals where adoption and investment are concentrating, and it highlights that instructors and managers are studied far less than students. The identified gaps, including newer tools such as ChatGPT, suggest areas where current evidence is thin, which can inform planning, procurement, and research priorities.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review followed PRISMA principles and protocol, identifying 138 articles from 2016 to 2022 for full examination. Data were extracted and coded using a priori and grounded coding. Publications rose nearly two to three times in 2021 and 2022 compared with prior years. Research spanned six continents, with leadership shifting from the US to China, and education departments becoming the dominant researcher affiliation. Undergraduates were the most studied group at 72 percent, and language learning was the most common subject. Five usage codes emerged: assessment or evaluation, predicting, AI assistant, intelligent tutoring system, and managing student learning.

papers.note: The paper argues that K-12 schools rarely weigh the ethical and societal costs of AI tools like facial recognition and automated assessment, and it offers teachers instructional resources from MIT and Code.org to help students understand AI and its dilemmas.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in education: Addressing ethical challenges in K-12 settings
papers.authors: Selin Akgün, Christine Greenhow
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how artificial intelligence is used in schools for things like personalized learning, automated grading, and facial recognition to understand student behavior. It says that while these tools can help students and teachers, schools rarely think carefully about the ethical and social problems they create. The authors explain what AI is, describe its benefits, and then point out the ethical dilemmas. They also suggest free teaching materials from MIT and Code.org so teachers can help students learn about AI and its ethical questions. The main message is that schools should consider both the good and the bad of AI.
papers.explain_business: This paper argues that K-12 schools often adopt AI tools like facial recognition and automated assessment without fully weighing their ethical and societal costs. For executives in education technology or school leadership, this signals a need to evaluate not just the promised benefits, such as personalized learning and teacher support, but also the ethical risks. The authors recommend using instructional resources from MIT and Code.org to teach students and teachers about AI ethics. The practical takeaway is that decision makers should include ethical review and AI literacy in their planning before or while deploying AI in classrooms.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors define AI through machine learning and algorithms, then survey educational applications such as personalized learning platforms, automated assessment, and facial recognition for behavior insights. They note that in K-12 contexts, the ethical and societal costs of these systems are seldom fully examined. The paper identifies ethical challenges and dilemmas, and recommends instructional resources from MIT Media Lab and Code.org to teach AI and ethics. The goal is to help practitioners gain the benefits of AI while navigating its ethical issues, and to provide teachers with materials to build students' understanding of AI and its ethical dimensions.

papers.note: Surveying 457 students and 180 staff in Hong Kong, this study proposes an AI policy framework for universities with pedagogical, governance and operational dimensions, giving educators a structured way to integrate AI responsibly across teaching, privacy and training.
papers.title: A comprehensive AI policy education framework for university teaching and learning
papers.authors: Cecilia Ka Yuk Chan
papers.explain_beginner: This study asked 457 students and 180 teachers and staff at Hong Kong universities about their views on text generative AI. From their answers, the author built a guide for how universities can use AI well. The guide has three parts. One part is about teaching and learning, so AI helps students learn better. Another part is about safety, privacy and who is responsible. The third part is about tools and training for staff and students. The guide matters because it gives universities a clear, organised way to bring AI into education responsibly, instead of leaving everyone confused about the rules.
papers.explain_business: For an executive, this paper signals that AI adoption in universities needs a structured policy, not ad hoc tools. Based on surveys of 457 students and 180 staff in Hong Kong, the author proposes a framework with three parts: teaching and learning, governance of privacy, security and accountability, and operations covering infrastructure and training. The practical takeaway is that institutions should decide on all three fronts together, because student and staff perceptions shape how well AI is used. This informs decisions about where to invest, especially in training and infrastructure, and how to assign clear responsibilities before scaling AI in teaching.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study surveyed 457 students and 180 teachers and staff across disciplines in Hong Kong universities, mixing quantitative and qualitative methods to capture perceptions of text generative AI. From this data the author derived the AI Ecological Education Policy Framework, structured along three dimensions. The Pedagogical dimension targets improved teaching and learning outcomes through AI. The Governance dimension covers privacy, security and accountability. The Operational dimension addresses infrastructure and training. The framework is intended to give stakeholders a nuanced grasp of AI's implications in academic settings, so they understand their responsibilities and can act accordingly. No specific effect sizes or interventions are reported in the abstract.

papers.note: This review finds that students who trust AI dialogue systems without question may lose critical thinking, decision-making and analytical skills, which matters as generative tools spread through classrooms and research.
papers.title: The effects of over-reliance on AI dialogue systems on students' cognitive abilities: a systematic review
papers.authors: Chunpeng Zhai, Santoso Wibowo, Lily D. Li
papers.explain_beginner: This review looked at how students use AI chat systems for school and research. When students accept what the AI says without questioning it, they may stop practicing important thinking skills. The authors examined 14 studies and found that this blind trust can weaken decision-making, critical thinking, and analytical reasoning. The reason is that people often prefer quick, easy answers over slower, more careful thinking. This matters because AI tools are becoming common in classrooms, so students need to learn when to trust them and when to think for themselves.
papers.explain_business: This review shows that when students trust AI dialogue systems without question, their critical thinking, decision-making, and analytical skills can decline. The authors analyzed 14 studies and found that over-reliance is linked to ethical issues around AI and to a preference for quick answers over careful reasoning. For organizations selling or deploying AI tools in education, this signals a need to design for appropriate trust, not blind acceptance. It informs decisions about training, guardrails, and features that encourage users to evaluate AI outputs rather than accept them automatically, protecting long-term cognitive skills.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines and analyzed 14 articles from ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science. It examined how students' over-reliance on AI dialogue systems with generative models affects decision-making, critical thinking, and analytical reasoning. Over-reliance was defined as accepting AI recommendations without question, often due to difficulty judging AI reliability or calibrating trust. The key finding is that ethical issues related to AI contribute to over-reliance, which in turn harms cognitive abilities. Users tend to favor fast, optimal solutions over slower ones limited by practicality, preferring cognitive shortcuts even when ethical concerns exist.

papers.note: A survey of 60 leading AIED researchers found most lack ethics training, so the field needs a multidisciplinary framework with robust guidelines to handle fairness, bias, transparency and unintended consequences in educational AI.
papers.title: Ethics of AI in Education: Towards a Community-Wide Framework
papers.authors: W. Holmes, Kaśka Porayska‐Pomsta, Ken Holstein, Emma Sutherland, Toby T. Baker, Simon Buckingham Shum, et al.
papers.explain_beginner: A group of researchers asked 60 leading experts in artificial intelligence and education about ethics. Only 17 replied. The answers showed that most experts in this field have never been trained to handle moral questions about their work. The paper argues that good intentions alone are not enough, because AI in education can still be unfair, biased, or have unexpected effects on students. The authors conclude that the field needs a shared ethical framework, built with help from many disciplines and clear rules, so that AI tools for learning are designed and used responsibly.
papers.explain_business: This paper signals that the AI in education field lacks shared ethical standards, and most researchers in it have no ethics training. For an executive, that means products built on this research carry unresolved risks around fairness, bias, transparency, and unintended effects on learners. The decision this informs is whether to wait for a community-wide framework or act now. A practical response is to require multidisciplinary ethics review and clear internal guidelines before deploying educational AI, rather than assuming good intentions are enough. This can reduce reputational, legal, and trust risks.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors surveyed 60 leading AIED researchers on ethics in educational AI, covering fairness, accountability, transparency, bias, autonomy, agency, and inclusion, and distinguishing between doing ethical things and doing things ethically. Seventeen responded. Their contributions surfaced complex issues, including the finding that most AIED researchers lack training to address emerging ethical questions. The paper frames this as a critical gap and proposes that a well-designed framework combining a multidisciplinary approach with robust guidelines is vital. The key result is the identified need for community-wide ethical infrastructure rather than relying on individual intentions.

papers.note: A review of 100 papers from 2010 to 2020 maps how AI in education moved from classification and recommendation toward adaptive, immersive and gamified learning, and warns that inappropriate use, shifting teacher and student roles, and ethical issues matter as much as the technology itself.
papers.title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Education from 2010 to 2020
papers.authors: Xuesong Zhai, Xiaoyan Chu, Ching Sing Chai, Morris Siu–Yung Jong, Andreja Istenič Starčič, Michael Spector, et al.
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looked at 100 studies about artificial intelligence in education, published between 2010 and 2020. The authors sorted the research into three groups: tools that classify or recommend things, tools that give feedback or adapt to learners, and tools that involve emotions, role play, immersive learning, or games. They found the field is moving toward more personal and interactive learning. They also warn that problems like misuse of AI, changing roles for teachers and students, and ethical concerns matter just as much as the technology. This helps readers understand both the promise and the risks of AI in classrooms.
papers.explain_business: This review of 100 papers from 2010 to 2020 shows that AI in education has shifted from simple sorting and recommending toward adaptive, immersive, and gamified learning. For leaders, the key message is that the technology alone is not enough. Inappropriate use, changing roles of teachers and students, and social and ethical concerns are just as important as the tools. This informs decisions about investing in AI for training or education, and it argues for pairing technology adoption with clear policies on ethics, teacher support, and student roles rather than treating AI as a purely technical purchase.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors performed a content analysis of 100 papers from the Social Sciences Citation Index education category, covering 2010 to 2020. Of these, 63 were empirical papers containing 74 studies, and 37 were analytic. Research questions were grouped into three layers: development (classification, matching, recommendation, deep learning), application (feedback, reasoning, adaptive learning), and integration (affection computing, role playing, immersive learning, gamification). Suggested future trends include the Internet of Things, swarm intelligence, deep learning, neuroscience, and assessment of AI in education. Reported challenges include inappropriate use of AI techniques, shifting teacher and student roles, and social and ethical issues.

papers.note: The paper maps international AI education policies and finds no single global consensus, proposing a synthesized set of ethical principles to guide students, teachers, developers and policymakers in building trustworthy AIED.
papers.title: Ethical principles for artificial intelligence in education
papers.authors: Andy Nguyen, Ha Ngan Ngo, Yvonne Hong, Belle Dang, Bich‐Phuong Thi Nguyen
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at the rules different countries and organizations have made for using artificial intelligence in schools. The authors compared these policies and found that there is no single global agreement on what counts as ethical. Because of this, they combined the ideas into one shared set of ethical principles. This matters because AI is being used more and more in education, and it can affect students' private data and their freedom to learn in their own way. The authors hope their combined principles will help everyone involved build AI tools that are trustworthy.
papers.explain_business: AI in education is spreading, and different regions follow different ethical rules, so there is no single global standard to rely on. This paper reviewed international policies and combined them into one set of ethical principles for AI in education. For executives, this means any AI learning product or institutional rollout should be checked against a shared ethical framework, not just local rules. The framework covers the interests of students, teachers, developers, policymakers, and institutional leaders. It informs decisions about which AI education tools to adopt, how to govern their use, and how to build trust with users and regulators.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors examined current policies and guidelines on ethical AI in education from international organizations to test whether a global consensus exists. They first reviewed the opportunities AIED offers and the ethical concerns it raises, such as issues around personal data and learner autonomy. They then applied thematic analysis to synthesize these policies into a conceptual set of ethical principles. The paper discusses each principle and its implications for students, teachers, developers, policymakers, and institutional decision makers. The resulting framework is intended to guide ethical and trustworthy development and deployment of AIED and to encourage future impact studies.

papers.note: A large urban school experiment found that an intelligent algebra tutor, built with teachers rather than imposed on them, raised student test scores well above comparison classes, showing that lab tutoring systems can work at real scale in ordinary high schools.
papers.title: Intelligent Tutoring Goes To School in the Big City
papers.authors: Kenneth R. Koedinger, John R. Anderson, William H. Hadley, Mary A. Mark
papers.explain_beginner: This paper describes a project that brought a computer tutor into real high school algebra classes in a big city. Teachers helped design the tutor and the curriculum, so it fit their goals and teaching style. In one school year, about 470 students used the tutor. These students scored 15 percent better than other classes on standard tests, and twice as well on tests about the specific topics they studied. The finding matters because it shows that computer tutoring can work in ordinary, busy city schools, not just in small experiments.
papers.explain_business: This study shows that a computer-based algebra tutor, developed with teachers rather than imposed on them, improved student performance in real urban high schools. Students using it scored 15 percent higher on standardized tests and twice as high on curriculum-specific tests. For decision makers, the lesson is that intelligent tutoring can be deployed at scale in ordinary classrooms and still produce measurable gains. It supports investing in tools co-designed with educators, and it suggests such systems can be a practical way to raise math achievement in large school districts.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors report a large-scale evaluation of an intelligent algebra tutor, PAT, embedded in the Pittsburgh Urban Mathematics Project curriculum, which emphasizes real world analysis and computational tools. The tutor was created through a client-centered design process, combining teacher curricular and classroom expertise with AI and cognitive psychology knowledge. PAT became part of regular 9th grade algebra in three Pittsburgh schools. In 1993-94, 470 experimental students outperformed comparison classes by 15 percent on standardized tests and 100 percent on PUMP-targeted tests, demonstrating technical and pedagogical scalability in urban high schools.

papers.note: This survey maps how educational data mining and learning analytics have grown since 2013, cataloguing methods, tools, datasets and trends, so AI in education researchers can see the field's current state and where it is heading.
papers.title: Educational data mining and learning analytics: An updated survey
papers.authors: Cristóbal Romero, Sebastián Ventura
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how researchers study data from education, such as information about students and how they learn. The authors updated an earlier survey from 2013 to show how much the field has grown. They describe the different names people now use for this work, the tools available, the free datasets, and the methods researchers apply. They also point to where the field is heading. It matters because it gives a clear picture of how data and AI are being used to understand and improve education, and it helps newcomers see the whole landscape in one place.
papers.explain_business: This survey shows that using data and AI in education has grown a lot since 2013 and now covers many areas, from academic and institutional analytics to teaching analytics and data driven decision making. It catalogues the tools, datasets, methods, and trends that define the field today. For an executive, this means the space is broad and maturing, so any investment or strategy in education technology should account for these many subfields and the free resources already available. The decision it informs is how to scope and prioritise AI in education initiatives using a clear map of the current landscape.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey updates a 2013 review on data mining in education. The authors give a general overview of how Educational Data Mining and Learning Analytics are applied to educational data. They cover the main publications and milestones, the knowledge discovery cycle, educational environments, specific tools, freely available datasets, commonly used methods, main objectives, and future trends. They also note the many related terms now in use, such as Academic Analytics, Institutional Analytics, Teaching Analytics, and Educational Data Science. The key result is a current state of the art that maps the field's growth and direction since 2013.

papers.note: The paper argues that educational data mining and learning analytics should collaborate more formally, sharing methods and tools, which matters because AI in education needs both communities working together to improve teaching and learning research.
papers.title: Learning analytics and educational data mining
papers.authors: George Siemens, Ryan S. Baker
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at two groups of researchers who study data in education. One group is called Educational Data Mining, the other is Learning Analytics and Knowledge. They grew up separately even though they work on similar problems. The authors say these two groups should talk to each other more and work together in a formal way. That way they can share their research, their methods, and their tools. This matters because better teamwork between them can lead to better research on teaching and learning, and stronger use of AI in education.
papers.explain_business: Rising interest in data and analytics across education has created demand for high quality research into models, methods, technologies, and impact. Two separate research communities, Educational Data Mining and Learning Analytics and Knowledge, have been serving that demand on their own. This paper argues they should collaborate formally and share research, methods, and tools. For an executive, the practical implication is that investments in education analytics may deliver more if they draw on both communities rather than one. The decision this informs is whether to support and fund collaboration between these groups instead of treating them as separate silos.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper addresses two distinct research communities, Educational Data Mining (EDM) and Learning Analytics and Knowledge (LAK), which developed independently in response to growing interest in data and analytics in education. The authors argue that this separation limits progress. Their position is that the communities should establish increased and formal communication and collaboration. The proposed benefit is the sharing of research, methods, and tools for data mining and analysis. This sharing would serve the development of both fields, EDM and LAK, rather than one borrowing from the other informally.

papers.note: The paper argues that AI in education can make learning processes explicit and give every student personalised tutoring, while augmenting rather than replacing teachers, which matters because it could address achievement gaps as smart machines reshape work.
papers.title: Intelligence Unleashed: An argument for AI in Education
papers.authors: Rosemary Luckin, W. Holmes
papers.explain_beginner: This paper explains what artificial intelligence in education is and what it could do for learning. The authors say AI can help make learning clearer and give every student one-on-one tutoring, in every subject, at a scale that was not possible before. It can also support students working in groups and in virtual settings. Importantly, the authors do not think AI should replace teachers. Instead, AI should work alongside teachers and make their expertise go further. The paper matters because this could help close achievement gaps and prepare people for a world where smart machines are changing jobs.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper signals that AI in education is not just a technology play, it is a strategy for improving learning outcomes at scale. The authors argue that well-designed AIEd can personalise learning, support teachers rather than replace them, and help address achievement gaps and teacher retention. It also responds to job displacement by smart machines, which raises the bar for what education systems must achieve. The practical decision this informs is to invest in collaborative, standards-based AIEd tools co-designed with educators, with funding focused on proven teaching and learning needs, not isolated experiments. The prize is better outcomes, but it requires new partnerships and ethical data use.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper has two aims: explain AIEd to non-specialists and argue for its role in teaching and learning. The authors describe AIEd as systems with human-like capabilities and behaviours, and as a scientific effort to make implicit knowledge computationally precise and explicit, opening the black box of learning. They report that existing tools can already provide one-on-one tutoring at scale, support group work, and create authentic virtual environments. Near-future expectations include lifelong learning companions and real-time assessment. The key argument is augmentation, not replacement, of teachers, with progress requiring a component-based infrastructure, shared data standards, and attention to pedagogy, technology, and system change.

papers.note: This position paper sorts AI in education into three paradigms, from AI directing learners to learners leading with AI, arguing the field is shifting toward learner agency and personalized, data-driven learning, which matters for anyone tracking how AI tools reshape teaching.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in education: The three paradigms
papers.authors: Fan Ouyang, Pengcheng Jiao
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how artificial intelligence has been used in education over time. The authors describe three stages. In the first, AI teaches and learners just receive. In the second, learners work together with AI. In the third, learners take charge and AI supports them. The paper argues that education is moving toward the third stage, where learners have more control and learning becomes more personal. This matters because it shows how AI tools may change teaching, shifting power from the system to the learner.
papers.explain_business: This paper argues that AI in education is moving through three stages, ending with learners in control and AI adapting to them. For leaders, the practical message is that products and strategies built around AI simply delivering content to passive students may become outdated. Instead, tools should support learner choice, personalization, and feedback loops where learner data informs the system. This informs decisions about where to invest in educational technology, how to design products, and how to prepare for a market that increasingly values learner agency and data-driven personalization.
papers.explain_practitioner: This position paper categorizes AI in education into three paradigms. Paradigm One uses AI to model knowledge and direct cognitive learning, with learners as recipients. Paradigm Two uses AI to support learning, with learners as collaborators. Paradigm Three uses AI to empower learning, with learners exercising agency. The authors argue the field is shifting toward the third paradigm, which emphasizes learner agency, personalization, reflection, and iterative, data-driven, learner-centered design. The key result is a framework describing this trend, not an experiment. It offers a lens for positioning AIEd systems and research.

papers.note: This review finds AI can help teachers plan, give feedback and assess essays, while teachers also train and check these systems, so it matters for anyone weighing AI's real classroom benefits against implementation challenges.
papers.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
papers.authors: İsmail Çelik, Muhterem Dindar, Hanni Muukkonen, Sanna Järvelä
papers.explain_beginner: This review looked at how teachers use artificial intelligence in their work. It found that AI can help teachers in three main ways. It can help them plan lessons by showing what students need. It can help during teaching by giving feedback right away. It can also help grade essays automatically. The review also found that teachers are not just users of AI. They help train it by acting as examples, and they check whether the automatic grading is correct. The paper also points out that using AI in teaching comes with challenges, so schools should think carefully before adopting it.
papers.explain_business: This review suggests AI can support teachers with lesson planning, real time feedback, and automated essay scoring, which could ease workload pressures in these areas. It also shows that teachers remain essential to making these systems work, since they help train the algorithms and verify automated assessments. For leaders, the practical message is that AI adoption in classrooms is not purely a software purchase. It requires teacher time and involvement, plus attention to implementation challenges. This informs decisions about where to pilot AI, how to budget for staff involvement, and how to set realistic expectations for rollout.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review examined research on teachers' use of AI applications and machine learning methods for analyzing teacher data. The authors report that AI supports three areas of teaching: planning, by identifying and communicating student needs, implementation, through immediate feedback and enabling teacher intervention, and assessment, via automated essay scoring. The review also identifies teacher roles in AI development, including serving as models for training algorithms and verifying the accuracy of automated assessment systems. Several implementation challenges in teaching practice are highlighted, and the authors present these as guidelines for future work in the field.

papers.note: The study develops an Intelligent-TPACK framework showing that teachers need both technological and pedagogical knowledge, plus ethics, to integrate AI well, since technical skill alone is insufficient for sound educational use.
papers.title: Towards Intelligent-TPACK: An empirical study on teachers’ professional knowledge to ethically integrate artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools into education
papers.authors: İsmail Çelik
papers.explain_beginner: Teachers are starting to use AI tools in classrooms, but this study says knowing how to operate the technology is not enough. The researcher built a survey to measure what teachers know about using AI for teaching, adding ethical questions to an existing framework called TPACK. The findings show that teachers who understand AI tools better also see more clearly how AI can help students learn. Technical skill helps teachers judge AI decisions, but on its own it does not make AI use work well in class. Teachers need technical and teaching knowledge together, plus ethics, to use AI soundly.
papers.explain_business: For leaders planning AI adoption in education, this research indicates that buying AI tools and training staff on their features will not deliver good teaching outcomes by itself. The study developed a measure of teacher knowledge for AI use and found that technical skill matters mainly when paired with pedagogical understanding, and that teachers also need ethics to evaluate AI decisions. The practical implication is that professional development budgets should fund integrated training covering technology, teaching method, and ethical judgment together, rather than standalone technical courses. This informs decisions about hiring, training design, and how readiness for AI integration is assessed.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study addresses a gap in teacher knowledge for instructional AI use. The author developed a scale based on the TPACK framework, extended with ethical aspects, to measure knowledge for pedagogically and ethically sound AI integration. A model was then built to examine how TPACK components and ethics interact. Results show that greater knowledge of interacting with AI tools relates to better understanding of AI's pedagogical contributions. Technological knowledge (TK) supports assessing AI decisions, but TK alone is insufficient. TK becomes meaningful for efficient AI deployment when combined with pedagogical knowledge (PK), expressed as technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK). The proposed Intelligent-TPACK framework reflects this.

papers.note: This paper traces how AI in education has developed unevenly, missing key links between research and practice, and argues that understanding this history matters for judging current claims about AI's role in teaching and learning.
papers.title: Historical threads, missing links, and future directions in AI in education
papers.authors: Ben Williamson, Rebecca Eynon
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how artificial intelligence has been used in education over time. The authors say this history has grown in an uneven way, and important connections between research and what actually happens in classrooms have been missed. They argue that knowing this past matters. It helps us judge the big claims people make today about AI in teaching and learning. So before believing that AI will transform education, it is worth understanding how it got here and what gaps still exist.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper is a caution about adopting AI in education based on hype. The authors show that AI's history in education has been uneven, with weak links between research and real practice. That means current promises about AI improving teaching and learning should be assessed with care. The decision this informs is whether to invest in or deploy AI tools now, and it suggests asking how past gaps between research and practice will be avoided. Understanding this history supports more grounded, evidence aware choices.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors examine the historical development of AI in education, describing it as uneven and noting missing links between research and practice. Rather than presenting new experiments or models, the paper traces how the field evolved and where connections broke down. Its key argument is that this history is essential for evaluating current claims about AI's role in teaching and learning. For engineers and researchers, the takeaway is that technical work should be read alongside its uneven past and the persistent gap between research outputs and classroom practice.

papers.note: This meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations found intelligent tutoring raised test scores by a median of 0.66 standard deviations, but gains were much larger on locally developed tests than standardized ones, so educators should weigh how test alignment and implementation quality shape reported effectiveness.
papers.title: Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems
papers.authors: James A. Kulik, J. D. Fletcher
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looked at 50 studies of computer tutoring systems, which are programs that teach students and adjust to their needs. On average, students using these systems scored better than those in regular classes, moving from the middle of the pack to the top quarter. But the size of the improvement depended on the test used. Gains were bigger on tests made by the local school than on standard nationwide tests. The authors also note that poorly run programs or weak comparison groups led to smaller gains. So how well a system is used and how it is measured both matter.
papers.explain_business: This analysis of 50 controlled studies shows intelligent tutoring can raise test scores substantially, with a median gain of 0.66 standard deviations, roughly moving an average student to the 75th percentile. However, results depend heavily on how success is measured. Gains were much larger on locally made tests than on standardized ones, and weak implementations or unsuitable comparison groups produced little benefit. For decision makers, this means pilot results can look better than real world impact if tests are not independent. Invest in proper implementation and use standardized measures to judge whether a tutoring system truly works before scaling it.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations of intelligent tutoring systems. The median effect was 0.66 standard deviations over conventional instruction, equivalent to a shift from the 50th to the 75th percentile. Effect size varied strongly with the outcome measure: locally developed tests showed larger gains than standardized tests, indicating that alignment between test content and instructional objectives shapes results. Two additional groups failing selection criteria were examined: six evaluations with nonconventional control groups and four with flawed implementations. Both showed small effects, suggesting control treatment design and implementation fidelity also influence reported effectiveness.

papers.note: A review of 118 papers finds 53 uses of large language models in education, from grading to feedback, but flags low readiness, poor transparency and weak privacy safeguards, so it urges open sourcing, newer models and human centred design.
papers.title: Practical and ethical challenges of large language models in education: A systematic scoping review
papers.authors: Lixiang Yan, Lele Sha, Linxuan Zhao, Yuheng Li, Roberto Martínez‐Maldonado, Guanliang Chen, et al.
